title: DBMS Notes — Part 1: Fundamentals
summary: A ten-page handwritten handbook covering database fundamentals: what a DBMS is, architecture and abstraction levels, data models and ER diagrams, the relational model, keys, SQL basics, constraints and relationships, normalization through 5NF, and transactions with ACID.

chapters.title: DBMS Introduction
points: Database: a collection of related data that is stored, organized and maintained to be easily accessed, managed and updated
DBMS (Database Management System): software that allows users to define, create, maintain and control access to databases
DBMS acts as an interface between users/applications and the physical database (Users/Applications -> DBMS -> Database)
RDBMS (Relational DBMS): stores data as tables (relations) made of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes)
RDBMS uses SQL (Structured Query Language) to manipulate and manage data
Example STUDENT table: ID, NAME, AGE, CITY with rows (1, Abhi, 22, Pune), (2, Rahul, 23, Delhi), (3, Neha, 21, Mumbai)
File System vs DBMS row: data redundancy and inconsistency vs minimizes redundancy
File System vs DBMS row: data isolation vs data independence
File System vs DBMS row: difficult data access vs easy and efficient data access
File System vs DBMS row: integrity problems vs integrity constraints
File System vs DBMS row: atomicity not guaranteed vs atomicity and consistency ensured
File System vs DBMS row: concurrent access problems vs supports concurrent access
File System vs DBMS row: security is weak vs strong security
File System vs DBMS row: no or limited backup and recovery vs backup and recovery available
Advantages of DBMS: reduced data redundancy, improved data consistency, data integrity enforcement, backup and recovery, data independence, efficient concurrency control
Tip: DBMS helps in managing large amounts of data reliably

chapters.title: Database Architecture
points: Database architecture defines how data is organized, stored, accessed and managed in a DBMS environment
1-Tier architecture: User/Application <-> Database on the same system; suitable for small, simple applications
2-Tier architecture: Client (User/Application) <-> Database Server <-> Database; client sends request to database server; common in desktop applications
3-Tier architecture: Client (User Interface) <-> Application Server (Business Logic) <-> Database Server <-> Database; presentation, application and data layers are separate; most scalable and secure
Schema (logical structure): the overall design of the database; does not change frequently (e.g. table structure, constraints)
Instance (actual data): the data present in the database at a particular point in time; changes frequently
Data abstraction hides unnecessary details and shows only relevant information to the user
Physical level: how data is actually stored (storage structure, files, indexes)
Conceptual level: what data is stored in the database and relationships (entire database structure)
External level: how different users view the data (multiple user views)
External Level (View Level) -> different user views (Student view, Teacher view, Accounts view) -> hides the details of how data is stored
Conceptual Level (Logical Level) -> entire logical structure of the database (tables, relationships, constraints) -> hides physical storage details from users
Internal Level (Physical Level) -> physical storage of data on disk

chapters.title: Data Models & ER Model
points: A data model is a collection of concepts used to describe the structure of a database, the relationships among data and the constraints
Data models overview: Hierarchical, Network, Relational, Entity-Relationship (ER), Object-Oriented, Object-Relational
ER Model: a high-level conceptual data model used in the early stage of database design; easy to understand and represents real-world scenarios simply
Basic components of ER model: Entity (a real-world object that can be identified), Attribute (property or characteristic of an entity), Relationship (association among two or more entities)
Entity: a distinguishable object in the real world; can be a person, place, thing or event; examples Student, Course, Department, Employee, Product, Customer
Attributes describe the properties of an entity; STUDENT example attributes: Name, Age, Gender, Roll_No, Email, Phone
Note: underlined attribute (Roll_No) in an ER diagram is the primary key
Relationship: an association among entities; types 1:1 (one entity related to one), 1:N (one to many), M:N (many to many)
Cardinality (degree) diagram: A —1— R —1— B, A —1— R —N— B, A —M— R —N— B
Total participation: every entity must participate in at least one relationship
Partial participation: some entities may not participate
ER diagram example (college system): STUDENT (Roll_No, Name, Date_of_Birth) —M— ENROLLS —N— COURSE (Course_ID, Title)
Symbol key: rectangle = entity, oval = attribute, diamond = relationship, double line = total participation

chapters.title: Relational Model
points: The relational model is the most widely used data model in DBMS; it represents data in the form of tables (relations)
Relation (table): a table with rows and columns; each relation has a unique name
Tuple (row): each row in a relation is a tuple; it represents a single record or entity
Attribute (column): each column in a relation is an attribute; it represents a property of an entity
Domain: the set of all possible values an attribute can take; example Age -> {0, 1, 2, ..., 120}
Degree (arity): number of attributes (columns) in a relation; a table with 6 columns has degree 6
Cardinality: number of tuples (rows) in a relation; a table with 150 rows has cardinality 150
Generic relation diagram: columns A1, A2, ..., An are attributes; rows v11..v1n through vm1..vmn are tuples
Relational schema: the blueprint or structure of a relation; notation Relation_Name(Attribute1, Attribute2, ..., AttributeN)
NULL represents missing, unknown or not-applicable values; NULL is not the same as zero or empty string
Example schema: STUDENT(Roll_No, Name, Age, Gender, Dept, Email) with Roll_No underlined as primary key

Example STUDENT table rows: (101, Abhishek, 21, Male, CSE, abhishek@example.com), (102, Pooja, 20, Female, IT, pooja@example.com), (103, Rohit, 22, Male, ECE, rohit@example.com), (104, Neha, 21, Female, CSE, neha@example.com)
Example facts: Degree = 6 (six attributes), Cardinality = 4 (four tuples); Roll_No domain = {101, 102, 103, ...}; Age domain = {0..120}
Key takeaway: the relational model is simple, structured and forms the foundation of RDBMS

chapters.title: Keys in DBMS
points: A key is an attribute or set of attributes that can uniquely identify a tuple (row) in a relation
Super key: any set of one or more attributes that can uniquely identify a tuple; a relation can have many super keys
Super key example: STUDENT(Roll_No, Email, Aadhaar_No, Name, Dept) has super keys {Roll_No}, {Email}, {Aadhaar_No}, {Roll_No, Email}, {Roll_No, Name}, {Email, Name}, ...
Candidate key: a minimal super key; no proper subset of it can uniquely identify a tuple; STUDENT candidate keys = {Roll_No}, {Email}, {Aadhaar_No}
Primary key: one candidate key selected to identify each tuple; cannot have NULL values; choosing Roll_No as primary key uniquely identifies each student
Alternate key: candidate keys not chosen as primary key; if Roll_No is primary key then Email and Aadhaar_No are alternate keys

Foreign key: an attribute (or set) in one relation that refers to the primary key of another relation; maintains referential integrity; in ENROLLMENT, Roll_No is a foreign key referencing STUDENT(Roll_No)
Composite (compound) key: a key formed by combining two or more attributes; used when no single attribute can uniquely identify a tuple; ENROLLMENT(Roll_No, Course_ID) is a composite key
Key hierarchy: Super Key -> Candidate Key (minimal super key) -> Primary Key (chosen candidate) -> Alternate Key (candidate keys not chosen)
Example STUDENT table: Roll_No / Name / Email / Aadhaar_No with rows (101, Abhishek, abhi@x.com, 1111), (102, Pooja, pooja@x.com, 2222), (103, Rohit, rohit@x.com, 3333); primary key Roll_No
Example ENROLLMENT table: Roll_No / Course_ID / Grade with rows (101, C001, A), (101, C002, B), (102, C001, A); composite key (Roll_No, Course_ID)

chapters.title: SQL Fundamentals
points: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language used to create, manage and manipulate databases
SQL is a declarative language; not case sensitive but conventionally written in UPPERCASE; end each command with a semicolon; works with RDBMS like MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server
SQL categories: DDL Data Definition Language, DML Data Manipulation Language, DQL Data Query Language, DCL Data Control Language, TCL Transaction Control Language

DDL defines or modifies database structure: CREATE TABLE Student (Roll_No INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(50), Age INT, Email VARCHAR(100)); ALTER TABLE Student ADD Column Address VARCHAR(100); DROP TABLE Student; TRUNCATE TABLE Student;
Gotcha: TRUNCATE removes all rows but keeps the structure; DROP removes the table completely

DML inserts, updates, deletes and manages data: INSERT INTO Student (Roll_No, Name, Age, Email) VALUES (101, 'Abhishek', 21, 'abhi@gmail.com'); UPDATE Student SET Age = 22 WHERE Roll_No = 101; DELETE FROM Student WHERE Roll_No = 101;

DQL retrieves or queries data: SELECT * FROM Student; with condition SELECT Name, Age FROM Student WHERE Age > 20; with sorting SELECT * FROM Student ORDER BY Age DESC; with limit SELECT * FROM Student LIMIT 5;
Tip: DQL is mainly the SELECT statement
DCL controls access permissions: GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON Student TO user1; REVOKE INSERT ON Student FROM user1; DCL ensures security by controlling user privileges
TCL manages transactions: COMMIT; makes changes permanent; ROLLBACK; undoes changes; SAVEPOINT sp1; then ROLLBACK TO sp1; rolls back to the savepoint
Basic SQL flow: Write Query (what you want) -> Execute Query (run on DBMS) -> Process (DBMS executes) -> Result (data / message)
Sample Student table: Roll_No / Name / Age / Email / Dept with row (101, Abhishek, 21, abhi@gmail.com, CSE)
Important points: always end SQL statements with a semicolon; use meaningful table and column names; SQL keywords are usually written in UPPERCASE

chapters.title: Constraints & Relationships
points: Constraints are rules enforced on table columns to ensure accuracy, consistency and reliability of data
PRIMARY KEY (PK): uniquely identifies each row; cannot be NULL and must be UNIQUE; syntax Roll_No INT PRIMARY KEY
FOREIGN KEY (FK): references the primary key of another table; maintains referential integrity; syntax Dept_ID INT, FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(ID)
UNIQUE: ensures all values in a column (or set of columns) are unique; syntax Email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE
NOT NULL: ensures a column cannot have a NULL value; syntax Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
CHECK: ensures values satisfy a specific condition; syntax Age INT CHECK (Age >= 18)
DEFAULT: provides a default value if none is specified; syntax Status VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'Active'
Referential integrity ensures a foreign key value must exist in the referenced table and prevents invalid data
Actions on update/delete: RESTRICT prevents the action; CASCADE propagates the change; SET NULL sets FK to NULL; SET DEFAULT sets FK to default
Referential integrity example: DEPARTMENT(ID PK, Dept_Name) and STUDENT(Roll_No PK, Name, Dept_ID FK); Dept_ID in STUDENT references ID in DEPARTMENT

One-to-one (1:1): each record in A relates to at most one record in B and vice versa; implemented with FK plus UNIQUE constraint; EMPLOYEE(Emp_ID PK, Name, Email, Passport_ID FK UNIQUE) <-> PASSPORT(Passport_ID PK, Passport_No, Issue_Date); each employee has one passport and each passport belongs to one employee

One-to-many (1:N): one record in A relates to many records in B; many records in B relate to one record in A; DEPARTMENT(Dept_ID PK, Dept_Name) 1—N STUDENT(Roll_No PK, Name, Dept_ID FK); one department has many students, each student belongs to one department

Many-to-many (M:N): many records in A relate to many records in B; implemented using a separate junction table; STUDENT(Roll_No PK, Name, Email) and COURSE(Course_ID PK, Course_Name) linked via ENROLLMENT(Roll_No FK, Course_ID FK, Enroll_Date); a student can enroll in many courses and a course can have many students

Constraints summary: PRIMARY KEY unique identification, allows NULL No, allows duplicates No; FOREIGN KEY maintain relationships, allows NULL Yes (by default), duplicates Yes; UNIQUE all values must be unique, NULL Yes, duplicates No; NOT NULL column cannot be empty, NULL No, duplicates Yes
Quick notes: PK = Unique + Not NULL; FK references another table; constraints prevent bad data

chapters.title: Normalization – Part 1
points: Normalization is a systematic approach to organize data in tables to reduce redundancy and avoid update anomalies
Functional dependency X -> Y: Y is functionally dependent on X (X uniquely determines Y); written as X -> Y
FD example in STUDENT: Roll_No -> Name, Age, Dept; Dept -> Dept_Name
Key rule: if two rows have the same value of X, they must have the same value of Y

Types of FD: Trivial FD (Y is a subset of X, e.g. Roll_No, Name -> Roll_No); Non-trivial FD (Y not a subset of X, e.g. Roll_No -> Name); Fully functional dependency (Y depends on the whole of X, not part); Partial dependency (Y depends on part of a composite key); Transitive dependency (Y depends on X through another attribute Z)
Insertion anomaly: cannot insert a fact without inserting another unrelated fact
Update anomaly: same data appears in multiple rows; updating one row may cause inconsistency
Deletion anomaly: deleting a row may cause loss of other important data

Unnormalized example table Roll_No / Student_Name / Dept_ID / Dept_Name / Dept_Phone: (101, Abhishek, D1, CSE, 011-1111), (102, Pooja, D1, CSE, 011-1111), (103, Rohit, D2, IT, 022-2222), (104, Neha, D3, ECE, 033-3333); problems: if Dept_Phone changes we must update many rows; if the last CSE student is deleted we lose Dept_Phone
1NF rules: all attributes must have atomic (indivisible) values; each column must contain values of the same domain; each row must be unique (use a primary key)

1NF example: not in 1NF (101, Abhishek, '9876543210, 9123456780', 'Java, Python'), (102, Pooja, 9988776655, 'C++, SQL') has non-atomic values; after 1NF each phone/skill combination becomes its own row (101 Abhishek 9876543210 Java; 101 Abhishek 9123456780 Python; 102 Pooja 9988776655 C++; 102 Pooja 9988776655 SQL) — now all values are atomic
2NF rules: table must be in 1NF first; no partial dependency; every non-key attribute must be fully dependent on the primary key

2NF example: table in 1NF with composite key (Roll_No, Subject_ID) and columns Subject_Name, Subject_Credit, Student_Name; Subject_Name depends only on Subject_ID and Student_Name depends only on Roll_No -> partial dependency

After 2NF: STUDENT(Roll_No PK, Student_Name), SUBJECT(Subject_ID PK, Subject_Name, Subject_Credit), ENROLLMENT bridge table (Roll_No PK, Subject_ID PK); now all non-key attributes are fully dependent on the key

chapters.title: Normalization – Part 2
points: Normalization continues with higher normal forms to remove transitive, multi-valued and join dependencies
3NF rules: table must be in 2NF; no transitive dependency; non-key attributes must depend only on the primary key

3NF example: ENROLLMENT(Roll_No, Student_Name, Dept_ID, Dept_Name, Dept_Location) with FDs Roll_No -> Student_Name, Dept_ID and Dept_ID -> Dept_Name, Dept_Location; transitive chain Roll_No -> Dept_ID -> Dept_Name, Dept_Location

Remove transitive dependency: Enrollment(Roll_No PK, Student_Name, Dept_ID FK) with rows (101 Abhishek D1), (102 Pooja D1), (103 Rohit D2) and Department(Dept_ID PK, Dept_Name, Dept_Location) with rows (D1 CSE Pune), (D2 IT Mumbai); now no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute; 3NF removes transitive dependency
BCNF: stronger version of 3NF; for every FD X -> Y, X must be a super key; eliminates anomalies caused by overlapping candidate keys

BCNF example: TEACHING(Teacher_ID, Course_ID, Course_Name) with FDs Teacher_ID -> Course_ID and Course_ID -> Teacher_ID, Course_Name; rows (T1 C1 DBMS), (T1 C2 OS), (T2 C1 DBMS); Course_ID -> Course_Name but Course_ID is not a super key, so not in BCNF

BCNF decomposition: TEACHING1(Teacher_ID, Course_ID) rows (T1 C1), (T1 C2), (T2 C1) and COURSE(Course_ID PK, Course_Name) rows (C1 DBMS), (C2 OS); BCNF requires every determinant to be a super key; BCNF removes anomalies due to multiple candidate keys
4NF rules: table must be in BCNF; no non-trivial multi-valued dependency; eliminates redundancy due to independent multi-valued facts

4NF example: STUDENT_HOBBY_LANG(Roll_No, Hobby, Language) with MVDs Roll_No ->> Hobby and Roll_No ->> Language (Hobby and Language independent); original rows (101 Cricket Java), (101 Cricket Python), (101 Music Java), (101 Music Python)

After 4NF decomposition: STUDENT_HOBBY(Roll_No, Hobby) rows (101 Cricket), (101 Music) and STUDENT_LANGUAGE(Roll_No, Language) rows (101 Java), (101 Python); Hobby and Language stored separately, no redundancy; 4NF removes multi-valued dependency redundancy
5NF (PJNF) rules: table must be in 4NF; no non-trivial join dependency; table cannot be further decomposed without loss of information
5NF example: SPJ(Supplier, Part, Project) with join dependency *(Supplier, Part, Project) — any two together determine the third, a non-trivial join dependency

5NF decomposition: SP(Supplier, Part) rows (S1 P1), (S1 P2), (S2 P1); SJ(Supplier, Project) rows (S1 J1), (S1 J2), (S2 J1); PJ(Part, Project) rows (P1 J1), (P1 J2), (P2 J1); joining these three recreates the original SPJ table without spurious tuples; 5NF removes join dependency anomalies
Lossless join and dependency preservation: a decomposition must allow rejoining tables without losing or adding tuples and must keep all functional dependencies checkable
Normalization goal: reduce redundancy and anomalies while keeping data recoverable through lossless joins

chapters.title: Transactions & ACID Properties
points: A transaction is a logical unit of work that must be completed entirely or not at all
Transaction concept: may read, update, insert or delete data; treated as a single unit of execution; either all operations execute successfully or none
Bank transfer example: transfer Rs 1000 from Account A to B = (1) debit 1000 from A, (2) credit 1000 to B; both steps must succeed otherwise the system should roll back

Transaction states: ACTIVE (transaction is executing) -> PARTIALLY COMMITTED (last statement executed) -> COMMITTED (committed successfully); ACTIVE or PARTIALLY COMMITTED -> FAILED on error/abort -> ABORTED (all changes undone) via roll back -> restart to ACTIVE
Atomicity (All or Nothing): either all operations in a transaction are completed or none; if credit to B fails, debit from A is also rolled back
Consistency (Preserve Consistency): transaction takes the DB from one consistent state to another; total balance of A and B remains the same after transfer
Isolation (Independent Execution): concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other; two transfers at the same time won't affect each other
Durability (Permanent Changes): once committed, changes are permanent even in case of failure; after commit data remains even if the system crashes

Transaction commands: COMMIT saves all changes permanently; ROLLBACK undoes all changes of the transaction; SAVEPOINT sets a point within a transaction; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes changes made after that savepoint; RELEASE SAVEPOINT removes a savepoint
Syntax example: SAVEPOINT sp1; -- do some operations; SAVEPOINT sp2; -- more operations; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1; RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp2;
Tip: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes changes after that point only

Lifecycle summary rows: ACTIVE + execute last statement -> PARTIALLY COMMITTED (all statements executed); PARTIALLY COMMITTED + COMMIT -> COMMITTED (changes saved permanently); PARTIALLY COMMITTED + ERROR -> FAILED (failure before commit); FAILED + ROLLBACK -> ABORTED (changes undone); ABORTED + RESTART -> ACTIVE (transaction starts again)
Practical bank transfer SQL: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE acc_no = 'A'; UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE acc_no = 'B'; COMMIT;
If any error occurs: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE acc_no = 'A'; error -> ROLLBACK; so the debit is undone
